segments.title: Personal accounts as remembered perspectives
segments.summary: Historians treat memoirs and recollections as perspectives on remembered events, then evaluate what each claim can support.
segments.body: Historians avoid reducing a personal account to a simple verdict of true or false. Each account records a person's perspective on remembered events. It may contain fallacies, serious inaccuracies, or a claim with no factual basis and still supply useful evidence. The way someone describes an event can reveal how they understood it, including information they did not intend to disclose. A binary label can hide that evidence. Historical analysis asks what an account can show even when parts of it cannot be trusted.

evidence.note: The introduction explains that every personal account is a perspective and may still reveal information when inaccurate.

segments.title: A memoir can preserve evidence of an internal debate
segments.summary: A junior officer may overstate who proposed an idea in a memoir while still showing that the idea was probably discussed within the organisation.
segments.body: A junior officer may later write, "I told my senior officer we must do this." In reality, the officer may only have raised the point, or someone else may have proposed it. The writer's claim to personal authorship remains uncertain. The memoir still suggests that the idea was probably discussed within the organisation. Historians can use that lead while withholding judgment about who first raised it.

evidence.note: A junior officer's memoir is used to distinguish an uncertain personal claim from evidence that an issue was being discussed.

segments.title: What a source's silence can reveal
segments.summary: When an account ignores an event, historians ask whether the writer lacked access to it or had a reason to conceal it.
segments.body: Silence in a personal account also creates questions for historians. Was the writer in a position to know about the event? If not, the omission may show how information moved, or failed to move, through the organisation. If the writer should have known, historians can ask why the event was ignored. The writer may have been hiding personal involvement or trying to avoid being tainted by it. An omission alone does not prove concealment, but the writer's access to information helps determine what the silence can show.

evidence.note: The transcript sets out questions about access to information, organisational circulation, and possible concealment.

segments.title: A provable lie can illuminate guilt
segments.summary: When evidence proves that a participant lied about an event, the lie may reveal guilt and an awareness at the time that the conduct was wrong.
segments.body: A third possibility applies when evidence proves that a participant was involved and lied about it. The lie then becomes evidence in its own right. It may indicate guilt, an attempt to escape responsibility, and awareness that the act was considered wrong even at the time. Historians can use that information when analysing both the event and the participant's understanding of it. The account remains useful despite the demonstrable falsehood.

evidence.note: A demonstrable lie is connected to guilt, evasion, and awareness that an act was wrong.
